vignette:
Arjun is a 68-year-old South Asian man, divorced, who works part-time for a small nonprofit organization focused on immigrant resettlement services. He was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure he made to his primary care physician, and he presented to the intake appointment with a PCL-5 score of 76, indicating severe posttraumatic symptomatology. What follows is a clinical portrait drawn from his self-report and the first two sessions.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Arjun was sexually assaulted - raped - by an acquaintance in his own apartment. He had invited the man in after a community event, someone he had known peripherally for years through the resettlement network. The assault occurred in his living room, late at night. He remembers the sound of the door being pushed shut, the particular creak of it, the sound of his own voice failing him when he tried to speak. He remembers pain - specific, located pain - and a silence afterward that felt absolute. He did not report the assault. He told no one for nearly a year.

In the months that followed, the memory did not behave like a memory. It returned without invitation, and when it did, Arjun heard things - the creak of that door, a low sound the man had made - as though they were happening in the room with him. Simultaneously, he felt pain in his body in the same places he had been hurt, a somatic replay that left him convinced, at times, that the assault was recurring. He has found, consistently, that he cannot adequately describe what happened; when he tries, the words dissolve before they form, and he sits in sessions with his hands open on his knees, knowing what he wants to say and unable to say it. These intrusive, sensory, and physically re-experienced memories have fed directly into his vigilance: after an episode of memory return, Arjun finds himself scanning his apartment for sounds that might mean someone is entering, listening at the threshold between sleep and waking for footsteps, for that specific creak. The memory, in other words, does not stay in the past - it continuously restocks his sense of present danger.

That sense of danger has become the architecture of his daily life. He startles violently when touched unexpectedly - a colleague at the nonprofit placed a hand briefly on his shoulder during a staff meeting, and Arjun stood up from his chair before he was conscious of doing so. He now positions himself at every meeting with his back against the wall so that he can see the entire room, and he has arranged his desk at the office accordingly. Loud or unexpected sounds - a door slamming in the hallway, a car backfiring near the resettlement center - send him into a state of high alert that can last for hours. This hypervigilance has, in turn, reinforced his belief that something is deeply wrong with him, that a man his age responding this way to a slamming door is beyond recovery, beyond dignity.

It is in the space of that belief that the most painful part of his presentation lives. Arjun has come to understand his reactions as evidence of permanent, irreversible damage. He is certain he will never feel normal emotions again - not warmth, not ease, not the quiet satisfaction he once took in his work with newly arrived families. He experiences himself as permanently outside ordinary human life, an outsider to the community he has spent decades serving. These appraisals - that he is a lousy coper, that he is fundamentally altered - have driven him to avoid being alone, and yet his divorce and his social withdrawal mean that he is alone most of the time, which intensifies both the vigilance and the despair. When the feelings become unbearable, he has, on several occasions, hurt himself physically - scratching or striking himself - because the physical sensation briefly interrupts the internal noise. He recognizes, with shame, that this behavior confirms to him everything he already believes about his inability to cope, and the shame itself sharpens his hyperarousal and brings the memory closer to the surface again.

What finally brought Arjun to seek help was a moment at work when a young refugee woman asked him a simple question about her resettlement paperwork and he could not respond - not because he didn't know the answer, but because he had, in that instant, entirely left the room in his mind. He drove home and sat in his car for two hours. He is most afraid, he says quietly, that he has become someone unrecognizable. What he is hoping for, though he struggles to say it, is to find his way back.
